claims.claim: Human-centered design is a process that starts with the people being designed for and ends with solutions tailored to their needs.
Human-centered design focuses on people and their context, seeks to understand and solve root problems, and continually prototypes, tests, and refines solutions so they truly meet people's needs.
The core principle is people first, design second: a user-centered process starts from user data, addresses real rather than imaginary user needs, and tests its designs with real users.

The classic process loop runs through phases — empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test — with implement as a sixth step in one formulation and inspiration/ideation/implementation as a three-movement compression in another.
The process is iterative and cyclical rather than strictly linear; teams often return to the understanding phases (empathize, define) after an initial prototype is built and tested.

The ideas behind human-centered design trace back to ergonomics and human-factors research and to the early computer era, when designers who overlooked human limitations produced systems that were hard to use; cognitive scientist Don Norman became a leading voice on designers' responsibility to users.

IDEO popularized the approach: its Design Kit describes human-centered design as the backbone of its work, and the related term 'design thinking' was coined in the 1990s by David Kelley and Tim Brown of IDEO together with Roger Martin.
The human-centered toolkit includes interviews, observation, and personas as methods for understanding the people a design serves; these methods are covered in their own lessons.

Human-centered design does not mean asking people what to build: users are poor predictors of their own future behavior, so designers should watch what people actually do rather than trusting stated preferences alone.
Solutions grounded in real needs are more likely to be used, because they solve problems that actually exist.
The U.S. federal government publishes a human-centered design guide series intended to enhance the understanding and practice of human-centered design across government services.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Different authorities describe the process with different numbers of phases.
positions: Nielsen Norman Group presents six phases: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test, implement (NN/g, read live 2026-08-21).
IDEO's Design Kit presents three phases: inspiration, ideation, implementation (IDEO.org, read live 2026-08-21).
The Interaction Design Foundation and the d.school-derived teaching tradition present five phases: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test (IxDF topic page, read live 2026-08-21).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the classic five-phase loop as the version most courses use, names implement as a sixth step in one formulation, and mentions IDEO's three-movement compression only in the history subsection. No claim is made that one formulation is the single correct one.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Human-centered design is sometimes equated with design thinking.
positions: IxDF treats design thinking as the broader concept that includes human-centered design, with HCD narrower in scope and aimed at making interactive systems usable and useful (IxDF, read live 2026-08-21).
NN/g treats design thinking and human-centered design as overlapping traditions sharing the same process loop (NN/g, read live 2026-08-21).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'human-centered design' for the process itself and mentions design thinking only in the history sentence about the term's 1990s coinage, avoiding a claim of identity between the two.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's boilerplate ('Human-Centered Design is a foundational concept in Ux/Ui Design') contained no verifiable factual content.
The draft's Eli-10 'label on a toolbox drawer' analogy was generic boilerplate and was replaced with an original library example.
The draft's vocabulary (context, evidence, application) was generic and was replaced with field-specific terms.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with a sourced working definition attributed to IDEO's Design Kit.
Grounded the history in IxDF's account of the early computer era and Don Norman, and in NN/g's account of IDEO's role in coining 'design thinking'.
Named the five-phase loop with one line per phase, referencing prototyping and testing to sibling topics.
Added the honest framing (understanding needs vs. asking what to build) grounded in Jakob Nielsen's stated-preference essay.
Added Digital.gov (GSA) as a Tier A government source for the adoption of HCD in public services.
Dropped any claim about the exact etymology of 'human-centered design' as a term; only the widely documented lineage (human factors, IDEO popularization) is asserted.

sourceRecords.title: Human-Centered Design — Design Kit (IDEO.org)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. IDEO.org's own description: human-centered design is a creative approach to problem solving and 'the backbone of our work at IDEO.org', a process that starts with the people being designed for and ends with solutions tailored to their needs, built on deep empathy, many ideas, prototypes, and sharing with the people being designed for; three phases: inspiration, ideation, implementation. Primary source for the attributed working definition and IDEO's role. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: What is Human-Centered Design (HCD)? — Interaction Design Foundation
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports the definition (focus on people and their context, solving root problems, continual prototyping/testing/refining), Don Norman's framing of HCD as a step above user-centered design, the design-thinking-vs-HCD distinction, and the history of early computing in which designers overlooked human limitations (1940s specialist-operated computers; 1980s personal computers used by non-specialists). Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Design Thinking 101
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports the six-phase framework (empathize, define, ideate, prototype, test, implement) with one-line descriptions of each phase, the iterative and cyclical nature of the phases (teams return to the understanding phases after an initial prototype is built and tested), the characterization of a user-centered process as starting from user data, addressing real rather than imaginary needs, and testing with real users, the quote that a wonderful interface solving the wrong problem will fail, and the history claim that the term 'design thinking' was coined in the 1990s by David Kelley and Tim Brown of IDEO together with Roger Martin. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: First Rule of Usability? Don't Listen to Users
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. Supports the honest framing: watch what people actually do, do not believe what people say they do, and do not believe what they predict they might do in the future; users do not reliably know what they want; stated preferences correlate only weakly with measured performance (r = 0.44 for applications, 0.53 for websites in later research). Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Human-Centered Design Guide Series — Digital.gov
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl on 2026-08-21. The HCD guides are intended to enhance the understanding and practice of human-centered design throughout the federal government, covering the discovery and design phases with concept and operations volumes. Confirms government adoption of HCD and lists method resources including interviews and personas. Facts synthesized; no prose reproduced.
